Substitute nalbuphine to avoid additive mu agonism
Hold methadone and use NSAIDs alone postoperatively
questions.explanation: Opioid-dependent patients need baseline plus surgical requirements.

questions.stem: A chronic-opioid patient's exact home regimen is unclear immediately before surgery. Which information should be established FIRST to prevent both withdrawal and unsafe supplementation?
options: Baseline daily opioid exposure and an appropriate equivalent dose
Whether regional anesthesia can eliminate every opioid requirement
questions.explanation: Calculate baseline opioid dose and equivalency.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient describes a burning electric component with allodynia in addition to nociceptive back pain. Which adjunct specifically targets the neuropathic component?
questions.explanation: Gabapentinoids help neuropathic pain.

questions.stem: A patient arrives in PACU after a long painful operation with severe uncontrolled pain and no transition analgesic plan. Which upstream failure MOST likely contributed?
options: Analgesia was not adequately planned and established before leaving the OR
Regional anesthesia concealed the pain until PACU
Excessive physiologic monitoring delayed opioid administration
questions.explanation: Poorly controlled pain leaving the OR may mean a long PACU stay.

questions.stem: A PACU clinician's observational estimate of pain differs substantially from a communicative patient's self-report. Which principle is most appropriate?
options: Use the patient's reliable self-report as a central measure and integrate function, behavior, and clinical context rather than assuming observer experience predicts accuracy
A novice clinician's estimate should replace self-report
An experienced clinician's estimate should replace self-report
Average the observer and patient scores
questions.explanation: Observers can both under- and overestimate pain. When a patient can communicate reliably, validated self-report remains central, supplemented by functional assessment and clinical context.

questions.stem: A patient reports pain 7/10, while an experienced nurse documents an impression of only 2/10 based on appearance. Which principle should govern treatment decisions?
options: The patient's report should remain central because experienced clinicians may underestimate pain
Clinical experience should replace patient self-report
The lower observer score should be used to prevent opioid exposure
Pain should be treated only when vital signs corroborate the nurse's estimate
questions.explanation: Clinician observation can under- or overestimate pain regardless of experience. When the patient can communicate reliably, self-report should remain central while function, sedation, respiratory status, and other clinical findings guide safe treatment.

questions.stem: After nerve injury, light brushing of the skin produces severe burning pain. Which sensory abnormality is present?
questions.explanation: Allodynia is pain from normally non-painful stimuli.

questions.stem: A patient after spinal cord injury has central neuropathic pain. Which therapy class may help?
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain may benefit from NMDA antagonists and gabapentinoids.

questions.stem: A patient has postherpetic neuralgia. What type of pain is this?
questions.explanation: Postherpetic neuralgia is a peripheral neuropathic example.

questions.stem: A patient has pain after stroke. What type is this?
questions.explanation: Pain after stroke is central neuropathic.

questions.stem: Immediately after a skin incision, pain is sharp, precisely localized, and confined to superficial tissues without electric or referred features. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: Superficial somatic pain is sharp and well localized.

questions.stem: After fracture repair, pain is dull, aching, and localized deep to the operative site in bone and surrounding tissues. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: Deep somatic pain is dull and poorly localized.

questions.stem: After laparoscopy, a patient has shoulder-tip pain despite minimal tenderness at the shoulder itself. Which mechanism BEST explains this pattern?
options: Referred visceral pain from diaphragmatic/peritoneal irritation
Superficial somatic pain from the shoulder skin
Direct neuropathic pain from surgical transection of the phrenic nerve
Deep somatic pain from shoulder muscle injury
questions.explanation: Visceral pain can be referred.

questions.stem: Four months after surgery, a patient still has pain at and beyond the operative site with no new acute injury. Which temporal classification now applies under the IASP definition?
options: Pain cannot be classified without proving neuropathy
questions.explanation: Pain lasting beyond 3 months is chronic.

questions.stem: Which drug class is recommended for nociceptive postoperative pain? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Nociceptive postoperative pain responds best to opioids and NSAIDs, along with acetaminophen. Anticonvulsants target neuropathic pain.

questions.stem: For a long spine fusion, an opioid-sparing infusion is desired but hypotension, bradycardia, and psychomimetic effects would be especially undesirable. Which adjunct in the source has a favorable serious-adverse-effect profile at studied doses?
questions.explanation: Magnesium lowers pain scores and opioid use without serious adverse effects at the studied doses.

questions.stem: A colectomy patient is at high risk for opioid-related ileus. Which expected effect makes perioperative IV lidocaine particularly attractive?
options: Reduced postoperative ileus along with opioid-sparing analgesia
Higher opioid consumption with faster bowel recovery
Longer hospitalization from delayed gastrointestinal function
questions.explanation: Lidocaine attenuates postoperative ileus.

questions.stem: During a subanesthetic ketamine infusion, a patient develops agitation with vivid perceptual disturbances despite stable ventilation and hemodynamics. Which drug effect best explains the change?
questions.explanation: Ketamine can cause emergence reactions and agitation.

questions.stem: During maintenance, blood pressure and heart rate rise with surgical stimulation and the pupils become dilated. Which interpretation BEST integrates these findings?
options: The patient has excessive opioid effect
Residual neuromuscular blockade is the most likely cause
questions.explanation: Dilated pupils and hypertension suggest inadequate analgesia.

questions.stem: Near emergence, a patient is restless and breathing 24/min after a painful operation. Neuromuscular recovery and oxygenation are adequate. Which action BEST addresses the likely analgesic component?
options: Carefully titrate short-acting opioid while reassessing ventilation and other causes of distress
Give naloxone because tachypnea indicates opioid excess
Reparalyze the patient to reduce respiratory rate
Deepen volatile anesthesia without reassessing analgesia
questions.explanation: Tachypnea and restlessness after a painful operation may reflect inadequate analgesia, but they are nonspecific. If other causes are excluded, cautious titration of short-acting analgesia with continued assessment of ventilation and arousability is appropriate; there is no universal respiratory-rate target.

questions.stem: Near emergence, a spontaneously breathing patient has RR 12/min, moderate miosis, adequate ventilation, and no signs of distress after opioid titration. Which interpretation best fits the combined findings?
options: A reasonable balance of analgesia and ventilatory effect
questions.explanation: A respiratory rate near 12/min with adequate tidal ventilation, gas exchange, arousability, airway protection, and no distress may be compatible with an acceptable opioid effect. A fixed respiratory-rate or pupil-size target alone does not establish safe emergence.

questions.stem: During emergence, hypertension from coughing is treated with a large opioid bolus just before extubation. Which complication is MOST likely after the airway is removed?
questions.explanation: Treating vital signs with opioids before extubation risks respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A PCA uses a 10-minute lockout despite a patient who frequently presses the button. What safety problem is the lockout primarily designed to reduce?
options: Dose stacking before the effect of prior doses can be assessed
Insufficient opioid exposure from patient control
The need to prescribe a basal infusion
questions.explanation: Lockout intervals prevent excessive dosing.

questions.stem: A PCA is set to hydromorphone 0.2 mg demand, 10-minute lockout, and a 4-hour limit of 4 mg. If the patient presses the button every time it is available, how much could he receive in 4 hours without the limit?
options: 4.8 mg, so the 4-hour limit caps him at 4 mg
2.4 mg, so the limit does not apply
8.0 mg, so the limit cuts his dose in half
1.2 mg, so the limit does not apply
questions.explanation: A 10-minute lockout allows 6 doses per hour, or 24 in 4 hours: 24 × 0.2 = 4.8 mg. The 4-hour limit caps the total at 4 mg.

questions.stem: A PCA order is missing the bolus dose. Which key variable is missing?
questions.explanation: Bolus dose is one of the five key PCA variables.

questions.stem: A PCA order specifies demand dose 0.2 mg hydromorphone. Which variable is this?
options: Lockout interval between successive patient demands
questions.explanation: The demand dose is the patient-activated dose.

questions.stem: A patient receives neuraxial morphine and is transferred to an inadequately monitored floor because ventilation is normal in PACU. Which complication may still emerge later?
options: Delayed respiratory depression from rostral opioid spread
questions.explanation: Neuraxial morphine can cause delayed respiratory depression requiring monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient has excellent neuraxial-opioid analgesia but develops intense pruritus and urinary retention without respiratory depression. Which management best preserves analgesia while addressing these adverse effects?
options: Consider very low-dose naloxone for pruritus and manage bladder dysfunction
questions.explanation: Pruritus often responds to naloxone; retention needs bladder management.

questions.stem: A patient remains hypoventilating after midazolam and fentanyl despite initial supportive measures. Which principle should guide further management?
options: Continue airway/ventilatory support and selectively titrate the antagonist that addresses the clinically important residual drug effect while considering reversal risks
Flumazenil must always be exhausted before naloxone can be used
Naloxone should be delayed until apnea occurs
Give another sedative to prevent awareness
questions.explanation: Airway and ventilation remain the priority. Flumazenil and naloxone are drug-specific antagonists and should be used selectively according to the suspected residual effect, severity, and patient-specific risks rather than a mandatory reversal sequence.

questions.stem: A patient taking naltrexone for opioid use disorder presents for painful surgery. Why can conventional opioid analgesia be unusually difficult?
options: Competitive opioid-receptor blockade can markedly reduce agonist effect
Naltrexone increases mu-receptor sensitivity and opioid potency
Naltrexone directly causes severe perioperative hypotension
Naltrexone potentiates NSAIDs enough to prevent opioid use
questions.explanation: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist, reducing opioid effectiveness.

questions.stem: A physically opioid-dependent patient receives a large naloxone dose and rapidly develops hypertension, diaphoresis, cramping, and agitation. Which mechanism BEST explains the change?
options: The patient developed isolated emergence delirium
questions.explanation: Naloxone can precipitate withdrawal in dependent patients.

questions.stem: A chronic opioid user needs progressively higher doses to achieve the same effect, with the dose-response relationship shifted rightward. Which adaptation does this represent?
questions.explanation: Tolerance shifts the dose–response curve right.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer has burning neuropathic pain. Which treatment principle is most appropriate?
options: Use multimodal therapy directed at neuropathic mechanisms; opioids may still contribute when pain is moderate to severe
Opioids are universally ineffective for neuropathic cancer pain
Neuropathic cancer pain should be treated with NSAIDs alone
Avoid adjuvant analgesics whenever opioids are used
questions.explanation: Neuropathic cancer pain often benefits from adjuvant agents such as gabapentinoids or antidepressants, while opioids may remain useful for moderate-to-severe cancer pain. Requirements vary and should be individualized rather than assuming a fixed higher opioid dose.

questions.stem: An older adult with peripheral neuropathy requires postoperative pain assessment. Which principle is most accurate?
options: Neuropathy can alter sensory perception, so pain assessment should be individualized rather than assuming a predictable age-related threshold shift
Peripheral neuropathy always raises pain threshold
Peripheral neuropathy always lowers pain threshold
Age and neuropathy make self-report invalid
questions.explanation: Aging and peripheral neuropathy can alter nociceptive processing, but effects vary by patient and disease. A universal increase in pain threshold should not be assumed.

questions.stem: A developmentally delayed child cannot self-report pain reliably after surgery. Which assessment problem is most important?
options: Pain and treatment response must be evaluated with developmentally appropriate behavioral methods
Children without self-report do not experience pain
Pain assessment is unnecessary without a numeric score
Vital signs alone reliably quantify pediatric pain
questions.explanation: Developmental and communication issues make pain evaluation difficult.

questions.stem: A 32-week preterm infant needs surgery for necrotizing enterocolitis. Does the infant need analgesia?
options: Yes, pain pathways are functional in preterm infants
No, pain pathways develop at term
No, preterm infants do not feel pain
No, pathways develop after birth and mature in infancy
questions.explanation: Preterm infants demonstrate nociceptive and stress responses and require appropriate analgesia. Development of pain processing is complex, so analgesic care should not depend on a single gestational-age cutoff.

questions.stem: A second analgesic modality is added because the first provides incomplete relief. What should happen to dosing and monitoring when the modalities have overlapping sedative or hemodynamic effects?
options: Reassess and titrate because combined therapies can compound adverse effects
Use full standalone doses because different mechanisms prevent interaction
Reduce monitoring because multimodal therapy is inherently protective
Increase each dose to ensure both modalities remain effective
questions.explanation: Take particular care when adding a second technique.

questions.stem: A patient with limited English proficiency cannot communicate pain quality or treatment preferences reliably because no interpreter has been used. Which barrier is most directly affecting care?
questions.explanation: Language and cultural barriers limit effective pain management.

questions.stem: A patient's family repeatedly refuses appropriate opioid rescue because they believe any perioperative opioid exposure inevitably causes addiction. Which barrier is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Opiophobia is fear of opioids and addiction.

questions.stem: A patient in PACU is anxious and reports high pain. What non-opioid intervention helps?
options: Reducing anxiety with reassurance or anxiolytics
Increasing the opioid dose without other measures
questions.explanation: Reducing anxiety is a listed non-opioid intervention.

questions.stem: During emergence, an otherwise ready-to-extubate patient reports throat discomfort and repeatedly reacts to the endotracheal tube. Which intervention removes the provoking stimulus when extubation criteria are met?
options: Give a large opioid bolus before extubation
questions.explanation: Extubation can reduce discomfort once criteria are met.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving a rectal analgesic. Which population is this route MOST useful for?
questions.explanation: Rectal analgesics are useful in small children.

questions.stem: An ambulatory patient has controlled pain, tolerates oral intake, and is leaving the facility. Which route is generally most practical for continued home analgesia?
options: Oral therapy, with transdermal treatment only when otherwise appropriate
questions.explanation: Oral and transdermal routes are helpful for discharge.

questions.stem: A patient has continuous wound infusion of local anesthetic. What route is this?
options: Continuous flow catheter within the wound
IV PCA delivered through the wound drain
questions.explanation: Continuous flow catheters deliver local anesthetic in wounds.

questions.stem: A patient with substance use disorder and complex chronic pain presents for major surgery. Which planning step is MOST appropriate before escalating perioperative opioids?
options: Consider consultation with a pain specialist as part of an individualized plan
Avoid all analgesia to prevent relapse
Use opioids without adjuncts to simplify management
Delay necessary surgery until all chronic analgesics are stopped
questions.explanation: Pain specialist consultation is recommended for high-risk patients.

questions.stem: A patient receives a detailed pain plan with documentation of goals. Which guideline is this?
options: Opioid-based management with fixed discharge doses
questions.explanation: Guideline 4 calls for individualized education and documented goals.

questions.stem: A multimodal plan provides good analgesia but causes troublesome nausea, sedation, and hypotension. Which response BEST reflects guideline-based reassessment?
options: Modify the regimen based on both analgesic adequacy and adverse effects
Increase opioid dosing because pain relief proves the plan is successful
Continue unchanged because adverse effects do not affect pain planning
Stop every analgesic rather than identify the contributing agents
questions.explanation: Guideline 6 says adjust the plan based on pain relief and adverse events.

questions.stem: A patient taking oxycodone 40 mg/day for chronic back pain presents for lumbar fusion after skipping the morning dose. Which immediate preoperative action BEST prevents withdrawal without attempting to treat the entire surgical pain burden?
options: Provide an appropriate equivalent of the missed baseline opioid requirement
Give a large intraoperative opioid bolus after induction instead
Use nalbuphine to replace the baseline mu agonist
Delay surgery solely because one scheduled dose was missed
questions.explanation: If the usual dose is missed, give an equivalent preoperatively to avoid withdrawal.

questions.stem: Case A: A 45-year-old taking oxycodone chronically is scheduled for lumbar fusion. How should her intraoperative and postoperative opioid requirement be anticipated?
options: Potentially higher than an opioid-naive patient's, but individualized after accounting for baseline exposure, surgical stimulus, multimodal therapy, and observed response
No different from an opioid-naive patient
questions.explanation: Opioid tolerance can increase perioperative opioid requirements, but the magnitude is highly variable. Maintain or replace baseline exposure and titrate additional analgesia to the procedure, multimodal plan, pain, function, and adverse effects rather than applying a fixed percentage.

questions.stem: Case A: A patient taking chronic oxycodone is scheduled for lumbar fusion. Which THREE strategies can appropriately reduce reliance on escalating full-agonist opioid alone? (Select 3)
options: Mandatory high-dose gabapentinoid regardless of risk
questions.explanation: Opioid-tolerant patients benefit from individualized multimodal therapy, which can include ketamine, regional/local techniques, and appropriate nonopioid analgesics. High-dose gabapentinoids are not mandatory and may increase sedation or respiratory risk.

questions.stem: An opioid-tolerant lumbar-fusion patient has severe pain despite escalating hydromorphone, with adverse effects increasing faster than analgesia. Which next principle is most appropriate?
options: Reassess the pain mechanism and multimodal plan; opioid rotation may be considered in selected patients rather than simply escalating the same opioid
Methadone is mandatory for all opioid-tolerant patients
Give naloxone to reset opioid receptors
questions.explanation: When escalating one opioid produces diminishing benefit and increasing toxicity, reassess the diagnosis and multimodal strategy. Opioid rotation, including to methadone in selected experienced settings, can be considered but is not universally required and requires careful equianalgesic conversion.

questions.stem: An opioid-tolerant patient taking oxycodone chronically needs PCA after lumbar fusion. Which PCA feature may be reasonable after calculating the patient's baseline opioid requirement?
options: A basal infusion plus patient-controlled demand dosing
Avoidance of PCA because chronic use implies addiction
Use of a mixed agonist-antagonist as the PCA drug
questions.explanation: Opioid-tolerant patients may need a basal infusion.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with severe COPD undergoes open upper-abdominal surgery. Which analgesic outcome is MOST important for reducing pulmonary complications?
options: Pain control sufficient for deep breathing, coughing, and mobilization
Sedation sufficient to reduce oxygen consumption overnight
Maximum systemic opioid dosing regardless of ventilation
questions.explanation: Regional analgesia promotes pulmonary toilet after upper abdominal surgery.

questions.stem: For the same severe-COPD patient after open upper-abdominal surgery, which technique BEST supports coughing and deep breathing while limiting systemic opioid burden?
options: High-dose morphine PCA with routine basal infusion
questions.explanation: Epidural analgesia supports pulmonary function and is superior to systemic opioids.

questions.stem: Case B: A 72-year-old with severe COPD had open upper abdominal surgery and has a thoracic epidural infusing. What must be arranged ahead?
options: Location, monitoring, and a team to manage the epidural
No monitoring beyond PACU once pain is controlled
Removal of the epidural in PACU before transfer
questions.explanation: Epidural planning includes postop location, monitoring, and follow-up.

questions.stem: An ambulatory knee-arthroscopy patient needs spinal anesthesia but rapid return of motor function is important for discharge. Which intrathecal strategy BEST balances these goals?
options: Low-dose bupivacaine with a small dose of lipophilic opioid such as fentanyl
A large lidocaine dose without adjunct
High-dose ropivacaine to prolong motor block
questions.explanation: Low local anesthetic dose plus lipophilic opioid minimizes motor block.

questions.stem: An ambulatory knee-arthroscopy patient is ready for discharge with controlled pain and oral intake tolerated. Which route best supports practical home analgesia?
options: Oral medications within a multimodal plan
questions.explanation: Oral routes are most useful for ambulatory discharge.

questions.stem: Case C: A 28-year-old woman is having knee arthroscopy as an outpatient. What education should she receive? (Select 3)
options: Taking extra doses if pain returns
questions.explanation: Education includes storage, disposal, and tapering.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old is crying and inconsolable after tonsillectomy but cannot provide a reliable numeric score. Which first step BEST avoids both undertreatment and reflexive oversedation?
options: Use an age-appropriate behavioral pain assessment and treat based on the full evaluation
Give naloxone because crying indicates opioid dysphoria
Sedate until crying stops without assessing pain
Discharge promptly because the environment is the likely cause
questions.explanation: Crying and inconsolability are pediatric pain expressions.

questions.stem: Case D: A 5-year-old is crying in PACU after a tonsillectomy, and his parents are highly anxious and tearful at the bedside. What is the BEST approach?
options: Engage the parents with family-centered care to reduce their stress
Remove the parents so the child calms down on his own
Ask the parents to wait outside until discharge
Give the parents sedatives so they stay calm at the bedside
questions.explanation: Family-centered care reduces parental stress, which helps the child.

questions.stem: Case D: A 6-year-old undergoes tonsillectomy. He is crying and inconsolable in PACU. Which route may be useful for this child?
questions.explanation: Rectal analgesics are sometimes useful in small children.

questions.stem: A known CYP2D6 poor metabolizer receives codeine after surgery and reports minimal analgesia despite adherence. Which mechanism BEST explains the failure?
options: Reduced conversion of codeine to its active morphine metabolite
Accelerated conversion of codeine to morphine causing rapid clearance
Enhanced renal elimination of morphine from codeine
questions.explanation: Poor metabolizers form little morphine from codeine.

questions.stem: A CYP2D6 poor metabolizer had inadequate analgesia from codeine. Which alternative avoids reliance on CYP2D6 activation for its analgesic effect?
questions.explanation: Hydromorphone does not need CYP2D6 activation, unlike codeine, tramadol, and hydrocodone.

questions.stem: A cesarean patient has excellent analgesia and normal ventilation in PACU after intrathecal morphine. Which postoperative plan is still required because of the drug's neuraxial kinetics?
options: Extended respiratory monitoring for delayed depression
No further respiratory monitoring if the PACU course is normal
Pain scoring every 8 hours without respiratory assessment
questions.explanation: Neuraxial morphine requires monitoring for delayed depression.

questions.stem: Two hours after intrathecal morphine, a cesarean patient has severe pruritus but remains alert with normal ventilation and excellent analgesia. Which treatment best targets the adverse effect while preserving analgesia?
questions.explanation: Pruritus from neuraxial opioids often responds to naloxone.

questions.stem: Eight hours after intrathecal morphine for cesarean delivery, a patient becomes somnolent with a respiratory rate of 7/min. Which mechanism BEST explains the timing?
options: Delayed cephalad CSF spread of hydrophilic morphine
Immediate systemic uptake of a lipophilic opioid
Opioid withdrawal as the spinal resolves
questions.explanation: Morphine's hydrophilicity causes delayed depression.

questions.stem: A patient receives dexmedetomidine, hydromorphone, and ketamine intraoperatively and reaches PACU bradycardic, hypotensive, and deeply sedated. Which explanation should be considered FIRST?
options: Additive or synergistic pharmacodynamic effects from the multimodal regimen
Isolated ketamine toxicity because ketamine predictably causes bradycardia
Residual neuromuscular blockade as the sole cause of hypotension
questions.explanation: Multimodal synergy increases side effects; lower doses when combining.

questions.stem: Dexmedetomidine, hydromorphone, and ketamine contribute to excessive sedation and hemodynamic depression in PACU. Which component lacks a routinely available human reversal agent?
options: A benzodiazepine, if one had been given
Rocuronium, if one had been given
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine cannot be reversed in humans.

questions.stem: A PACU patient reports 8/10 abdominal pain with HR 120/min, BP 88/50 mm Hg, and increasing abdominal distension. Which action takes priority over additional opioid?
options: Evaluate urgently for bleeding and hypovolemia
Give hydromorphone because severe pain explains all three findings
Give ketorolac to avoid opioid hypotension
Treat tachycardia with a beta blocker before investigating the abdomen
questions.explanation: Rule out bleeding and hypovolemia before treating pain.

questions.stem: The same patient is confirmed to be hypovolemic. Why can a large opioid dose produce further hemodynamic deterioration?
options: Reducing pain-driven sympathetic tone and causing vasodilation can unmask or worsen hypotension
Mu agonism markedly increases myocardial contractility
questions.explanation: Analgesia reduces sympathetic tone and can unmask hypovolemia.

questions.stem: After thoracotomy, a patient has severe dynamic pain, splints with inspiration, and cannot cough effectively. Which analgesic strategy BEST addresses both pain and pulmonary function?
options: Thoracic epidural or paravertebral regional analgesia
IV morphine titrated until the patient sleeps
questions.explanation: Regional techniques improve pulmonary function after thoracotomy.

questions.stem: After open upper-abdominal surgery, poorly controlled pain causes splinting and ineffective cough; pneumonia develops later. Which pain-related mechanism most directly contributed?
options: Pain limited deep inspiration and airway clearance
questions.explanation: Poor analgesia reduces pulmonary toilet and increases pneumonia risk.

questions.stem: A remifentanil infusion is stopped at the end of an ENT procedure and the patient is extubated into severe pain despite a smooth intraoperative course. Which planning failure MOST directly explains this?
options: No longer-acting transition analgesia was established before remifentanil offset
Delayed respiratory depression masked pain until extubation
questions.explanation: Remifentanil's short CSHT requires transitional analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient receiving remifentanil for ENT surgery is approaching emergence with substantial expected postoperative pain. Which transition plan best prevents severe pain when the infusion stops?
options: Establish longer-acting opioid and/or nonopioid analgesia before discontinuing remifentanil
Continue remifentanil routinely on an unmonitored ward
Avoid all opioids because ENT surgery carries airway risk
questions.explanation: Plan transitional analgesia for remifentanil cases.

questions.stem: A PACU patient is shivering, nauseated, retching, and reporting severe pain. Which approach BEST avoids unnecessary opioid escalation?
options: Treat temperature-related discomfort and PONV, then reassess the residual pain
Escalate opioid first because every distress behavior represents pain
Give naloxone because nausea proves opioid excess
Delay warming until the pain score is zero
questions.explanation: PONV and fever/temperature issues are pain differentials.

questions.stem: Case K: After treating PONV, pain remains 7/10. What is the BEST approach?
options: Nonpharmacologic measures alone until the next assessment
questions.explanation: Multimodal analgesia with titration is recommended.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient already has substantial central sensitization before surgery. Which limitation of preventive analgesia should shape expectations?
options: Blocking new perioperative nociceptive input cannot fully prevent sensitization that already exists
Preexisting sensitization makes preventive analgesia more effective
Preventive analgesia becomes unnecessary once chronic pain develops
Preventive analgesia predictably worsens chronic pain
questions.explanation: Pre-existing sensitization reduces response.

questions.stem: Case L: A patient with chronic pain has preexisting sensitization. What plan should be prioritized for this patient?
options: Opioids alone, titrated to comfort in PACU
questions.explanation: Chronic pain patients benefit most from multimodal and regional techniques.

questions.stem: Dexmedetomidine contributes to delayed awakening after a prolonged infusion. Which limitation prevents rapid pharmacologic reversal of its sedative effect?
options: No routinely available reversal agent exists for humans
Its only limitation is an extremely long elimination half-life
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine cannot be reversed.

questions.stem: A dexmedetomidine infusion contributes to delayed emergence after a long case. Which future planning change BEST addresses the problem without abandoning the drug entirely?
options: Adjust infusion dose and discontinuation timing to its duration-dependent recovery profile
Increase the infusion near closure to accelerate clearance
Begin the infusion only after PACU arrival
Avoid every sedative adjunct in future anesthetics
questions.explanation: Timing of drip stop matters to avoid prolonged emergence.

questions.stem: A protocol specifies a magnesium loading dose of 50 mg/kg. What loading dose does that protocol calculate for a 90 kg patient?
questions.explanation: 50 mg/kg × 90 kg = 4,500 mg = 4.5 g. This is a calculation exercise; actual perioperative magnesium regimens are individualized.

questions.stem: A protocol specifies a magnesium infusion of 8 mg/kg/hr. What rate does that protocol calculate for a 90 kg patient?
questions.explanation: 8 mg/kg/hr × 90 kg = 720 mg/hr. The calculation does not imply that this rate is appropriate for every patient.

questions.stem: A protocol specifies a ketamine bolus of 0.2 mg/kg. What bolus does that protocol calculate for a 50 kg patient?
questions.explanation: 0.2 mg/kg × 50 kg = 10 mg. Clinical subanesthetic ketamine dosing varies by indication and protocol.

questions.stem: A protocol specifies ketamine 0.15 mg/kg/hr. What infusion rate does that protocol calculate for a 50 kg patient?
questions.explanation: 0.15 mg/kg/hr × 50 kg = 7.5 mg/hr. Clinical infusion rates should be individualized.

questions.stem: Case P: A patient receives a block with 25 mL 0.5% ropivacaine. What is the dose?
Case P: The surgeon adds 20 mL 0.25% ropivacaine. What is the added dose?
A patient scheduled for inguinal hernia repair asks why long-term pain is discussed for a relatively routine operation. Which response is MOST accurate?
options: Inguinal herniorrhaphy is among procedures associated with chronic postsurgical pain
Chronic postsurgical pain occurs only after amputations
Hernia repair has no recognized chronic-pain risk
Chronic pain is limited to oncologic surgery
questions.explanation: Inguinal herniorrhaphy is among procedures associated with chronic postsurgical pain.

questions.stem: For a procedure associated with chronic postsurgical pain, which preventive strategy is MOST consistent with limiting central sensitization?
options: Provide analgesia with sufficient depth and field coverage that extends into the postoperative period
Avoid perioperative analgesia to prevent tolerance
Wait until emergence to begin opioid therapy
Avoid regional techniques because they mask early chronic pain
questions.explanation: Preventive analgesia aims to block central sensitization.

questions.stem: An older adult with mild cognitive impairment becomes intermittently confused after repeated opioid doses. Which age-related concern should MOST influence further treatment?
options: Greater vulnerability to oversedation and delirium requires cautious titration and reassessment
Older age reliably produces opioid tolerance
Higher pain tolerance requires larger routine opioid doses
Faster drug metabolism shortens every opioid effect
questions.explanation: Elderly patients have altered drug metabolism and cognitive vulnerability.

questions.stem: Case R: A 68-year-old has mild cognitive impairment and is receiving opioids. What approach is BEST?
options: Lower doses, careful titration, and multimodal adjuncts
Standard adult doses, since pain threshold rises with age
questions.explanation: Titrate carefully in geriatric patients.

questions.stem: A patient taking an SSRI becomes agitated and tachycardic after tramadol. Which pharmacologic property makes this combination concerning?
options: Tramadol has serotonergic/norepinephrine reuptake effects in addition to opioid activity
Tramadol is a pure mu agonist with no monoamine effect
Tramadol directly antagonizes SSRIs and precipitates opioid withdrawal
Tramadol is a local anesthetic that causes systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Tramadol has SNRI activity and interactions.

questions.stem: Case S: The patient on an SSRI developed agitation and tachycardia after tramadol. What lesson applies to tramadol?
options: It is safe with all antidepressants
It is a pure mu agonist with no monoamine activity
questions.explanation: Tramadol has SNRI activity and CYP2D6 dependence, creating many interactions.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient arrives for surgery with a PCA already in use. Before adding anesthetic opioids, which information is MOST important?
options: Recent delivered doses and timing, along with the current PCA regimen
Only the programmed settings, regardless of doses actually received
questions.explanation: Know last dose/time of analgesics that affect your plan.

questions.stem: Case T: A patient with chronic pain arrives on a PCA. What is the risk of ignoring prior PCA dosing?
options: Oversedation or withdrawal due to mismatched dosing
No change in outcomes, since the OR plan overrides PCA
questions.explanation: Prior dosing affects safety and effectiveness of your plan.

questions.stem: After laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a patient has shoulder-tip pain without shoulder injury. Which mechanism BEST explains the symptom?
options: Referred visceral pain from diaphragmatic/peritoneal irritation
Superficial somatic pain from shoulder skin
Peripheral neuropathy from surgical transection at the shoulder
Deep somatic pain from bone injury
questions.explanation: Visceral pain can be referred to the shoulder.

questions.stem: Case U: A patient undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy and has referred shoulder pain. Which intervention may help?
options: Stop all analgesics until the pain localizes
questions.explanation: Nonpharmacologic interventions and multimodal analgesia help.

questions.stem: Soon after neuraxial fentanyl, a patient develops clinically significant hypoventilation. Which response has priority?
options: Support ventilation and titrate naloxone if opioid reversal is required
Wait because only delayed respiratory depression is clinically important
Administer more fentanyl to prevent withdrawal
Give flumazenil as the opioid antagonist
questions.explanation: Early respiratory depression from fentanyl needs airway support and possible naloxone.

questions.stem: Clinically significant respiratory depression occurs soon after neuraxial fentanyl. Which property explains why the effect tends to appear early rather than many hours later?
options: High lipophilicity promotes rapid tissue/systemic uptake
Hydrophilicity promotes slow cephalad CSF spread
Slow metabolism creates delayed rostral migration
questions.explanation: Lipophilic opioids act quickly.

questions.stem: Case W: A patient has pain and hypertension after a tourniquet. What should you do first?
options: Assess for tourniquet pain and treat appropriately
Increase fluids, since hypertension reflects hypovolemia
Treat as expected hypertension and continue
questions.explanation: Assess pain source; tourniquet pain is common.

questions.stem: A patient with tourniquet discomfort becomes hypertensive but is also newly hypoxemic. Which problem takes priority before escalating analgesia?
options: Give opioid first because hypertension proves pain is primary
Give NSAID first because it cannot affect ventilation
Treat the blood pressure without addressing oxygenation
questions.explanation: Hypoxemia is a pain differential to treat first.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on methadone has an unexpectedly variable response to perioperative dosing despite adherence. Which property of methadone most complicates prediction of dose and effect?
options: Wide interpatient variability in pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and elimination half-life
Absence of clinically important drug interactions
questions.explanation: Methadone has substantial interpatient variability in metabolism, effect, and elimination half-life, with important drug interactions. Its behavior should not be reduced to a single CYP2D6 or genetic explanation.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on methadone presents for a painful operation. Which strategy BEST separates maintenance therapy from the additional surgical analgesic requirement?
options: Continue baseline methadone and add individualized multimodal perioperative analgesia
Stop all opioids until postoperative pain is measurable
Use acetaminophen alone because maintenance methadone covers surgical pain
questions.explanation: Continue baseline opioid and add multimodal analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient reports a 'morphine allergy' consisting only of prior generalized itching without swelling, bronchospasm, or hypotension. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Clarify and document the reaction as a likely opioid adverse effect rather than automatically labeling anaphylaxis
Treat the historical event as active anaphylaxis
Give prophylactic epinephrine before any opioid
questions.explanation: Isolated opioid-associated pruritus is commonly a pharmacologic adverse effect or non-IgE-mediated histamine-related reaction rather than IgE-mediated anaphylaxis. The exact historical features should be clarified and documented.

questions.stem: A patient previously labeled 'morphine allergic' now reports that the historical reaction included facial swelling rather than isolated itching. How should this new information change the assessment?
options: It raises concern for a potentially serious hypersensitivity reaction and warrants further evaluation
It confirms a routine opioid adverse effect only
questions.explanation: Facial swelling/angioedema is more concerning than isolated pruritus and warrants careful evaluation of the original reaction and alternatives. It raises concern for serious hypersensitivity but does not by itself prove an IgE-mediated opioid allergy.

questions.stem: A PACU patient reports pain 8/10 but repeatedly falls asleep and has a respiratory rate of 8/min after opioid therapy. Which action BEST balances the pain report with immediate safety?
options: Reassess arousal and ventilation and withhold further opioid until respiratory safety is established
Give a large opioid bolus because self-reported pain always overrides sedation
Administer naloxone automatically without assessing ventilation
Ignore the pain score because sleeping proves the patient is comfortable
questions.explanation: Reassess arousal and respiratory status before giving more.

questions.stem: Case Z: A patient in PACU has pain and a pain score of 8, but is sleeping and RR 8. What does this scenario illustrate?
options: Pain scores are accurate even when asleep
questions.explanation: Continuous reassessment prevents over-administration.

questions.stem: A severely anxious PACU patient hyperventilates and reports 10/10 pain despite substantial opioid already producing adequate analgesic exposure. Which next step BEST avoids compounding opioid toxicity?
options: Address anxiety with reassurance and an appropriate nonopioid/anxiolytic strategy while reassessing pain
Continue escalating opioid until the patient sleeps
Withhold all treatment because anxiety invalidates the pain report
Remove monitoring to reduce environmental stimulation
questions.explanation: Anxiety amplifies pain, and treating it is a non-opioid intervention.

questions.stem: Despite a structured multimodal plan, a high-risk patient continues to have difficult-to-control pain with complex chronic opioid exposure. Which systems resource should be available?
questions.explanation: Guideline 7 supports pain specialist consultation.

questions.stem: An epidural that had provided good analgesia stops functioning and breakthrough pain develops. Which next step BEST avoids compounding toxicity from a rescue modality?
options: Reassess the epidural and patient, then add or change therapy with attention to overlapping effects
Increase every epidural medication without checking the catheter or block
Stop all analgesia to determine the true pain score
Give naloxone before troubleshooting the epidural
questions.explanation: Adding a second modality requires care.

questions.stem: A patient becomes apneic after receiving both opioid and benzodiazepine. Which intervention takes priority before deciding which reversal drug to use?
questions.explanation: Airway support comes first; reversal may follow.

questions.stem: During an IV lidocaine infusion, a patient reports new circumoral numbness and metallic taste. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Suspect early local-anesthetic systemic toxicity, stop the infusion, and assess immediately
Continue because these are expected analgesic endpoints
Treat empirically for hypocalcemia without changing lidocaine
questions.explanation: Perioral numbness suggests LAST; stop the infusion and assess.

questions.stem: A peripheral nerve block is proposed in a room without immediate airway/resuscitation equipment or lipid emulsion. Which safety concern should determine whether to proceed?
options: A serious block complication could occur before rescue resources arrive
Remote placement reduces complications because there are fewer interruptions
Emergency equipment is unnecessary for ultrasound-guided blocks
Lowering the local-anesthetic dose eliminates the need for rescue capability
questions.explanation: Regional anesthesia requires emergency equipment.

questions.stem: During a low-dose ketamine infusion, a patient remains hemodynamically stable but develops vivid dreams and perceptual disturbances. Which drug effect best explains the symptoms?
questions.explanation: Ketamine can cause dissociative effects.

questions.stem: During a magnesium analgesic infusion, a patient shows greater-than-expected weakness after a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Which interaction should be suspected?
options: Acute opioid tolerance caused by magnesium
questions.explanation: Magnesium can enhance neuromuscular blockade and weakness.

questions.stem: A patient wearing a transdermal fentanyl patch is placed under an active warming device during a long operation. Which pharmacokinetic concern is MOST important?
options: Heat can increase transdermal fentanyl absorption and opioid exposure
questions.explanation: Warming can increase transdermal absorption, raising opioid levels.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient with severe anxiety and PTSD is scheduled for major surgery. Why should these comorbidities be addressed in the perioperative pain plan?
options: Psychological comorbidity can amplify pain experience and complicate analgesic management
Psychiatric symptoms should be deferred until surgical pain resolves
Opioids alone reliably treat both chronic pain and PTSD
Regional techniques are contraindicated when anxiety is present
questions.explanation: Managing anxiety, PTSD, and depression is part of effective pain care in chronic pain patients.

questions.stem: After spine surgery, a patient describes burning pain radiating down the leg with electric shocks and allodynia. Which mechanism should be specifically targeted in addition to routine incisional analgesia?
questions.explanation: Burning and radiating pain suggests neuropathic features.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient reports that pain is tolerable at rest but becomes severe with coughing. In a structured pain history, how should coughing be classified?
questions.explanation: Exacerbating factors make pain start or worsen.

questions.stem: A patient reports that applying ice consistently decreases incisional pain. In a structured pain assessment, what does this identify?
questions.explanation: Relieving factors make pain better.

questions.stem: A patient says postoperative pain prevents walking to the bathroom despite tolerable pain at rest. Which assessment domain is most directly affected?
options: Interference with function and activities of daily living
questions.explanation: Pain assessment includes interference with ADLs.

questions.stem: After hernia repair, a patient is diaphoretic and nauseated but reports pain 2/10. Which interpretation BEST avoids unnecessary opioid administration?
options: Autonomic and gastrointestinal signs are nonspecific and may have causes other than pain
Sweating and nausea prove severe pain despite the patient's report
Patient self-report should be ignored when autonomic signs are present
Nausea is the most specific physiologic measure of postoperative pain
questions.explanation: Nausea and sweating may reflect other causes, so the patient's report is preferred.

questions.stem: A unit routinely substitutes clinicians' visual estimates for patient-reported pain scores. Which error is MOST likely?
options: Systematic observer bias related to experience and assumptions
More accurate assessment than patient self-report
Elimination of cultural influences on pain assessment
questions.explanation: Staff estimates are biased by experience, so patient self-report is preferred.

questions.stem: A patient's pain management plan is agreed on by patient, surgeon, and anesthesia. Which note principle is this?
options: Plan developed in the PACU after emergence
questions.explanation: The plan should be agreed on by patient, surgeon, and anesthesia.

questions.stem: A thoracic epidural will require a higher-acuity postoperative location and specialized follow-up. When should these resources be secured?
options: Before surgery as part of the analgesic plan
After PACU arrival if the epidural still works
Only after the first breakthrough-pain episode
questions.explanation: Extended plans need coordination before entering the OR.

questions.stem: A patient receiving repeated opioids develops constipation without signs of withdrawal or another acute abdominal process. How should this finding be classified?
questions.explanation: Constipation is a listed adverse effect.

questions.stem: A patient has anaphylaxis after an analgesic. Which category is this?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a listed adverse effect.

questions.stem: After neuraxial and systemic opioid exposure, a patient develops suprapubic fullness and inability to void. Which response best addresses this recognized opioid adverse effect?
options: Assess bladder volume and manage urinary retention
Ignore it because retention is always self-limited
questions.explanation: Urinary retention is a listed adverse effect; manage appropriately.

questions.stem: After colectomy, morphine monotherapy controls pain poorly and causes severe nausea and constipation. Which change BEST improves the therapeutic balance?
options: Add nonopioid and/or regional multimodal strategies to reduce opioid requirement
Increase morphine and add a basal PCA infusion
Stop antiemetics so nausea can guide opioid titration
Avoid all nonopioid agents to prevent drug interactions
questions.explanation: Multimodal combinations lower opioid doses and their side effects.

questions.stem: A patient's pain is controlled with acetaminophen and NSAIDs. What does this demonstrate?
options: Improved analgesia and reduced opioid consumption
Higher respiratory depression risk from the combination
questions.explanation: Combining acetaminophen with NSAIDs improves analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient with significant renal impairment is receiving ketorolac as part of a multimodal regimen. Which adjustment is MOST appropriate?
options: Reconsider the NSAID and use renal-appropriate multimodal alternatives
Increase ketorolac because renal impairment reduces its effect
Continue the standard regimen without reassessment
Add morphine specifically to protect renal function
questions.explanation: NSAIDs may be limited in renal impairment; choose alternatives.

questions.stem: A 75-kg patient has received no other local anesthetic. The surgeon requests 30 mL of 1% plain lidocaine. Using a maximum of about 4.5 mg/kg, which assessment is correct?
options: 300 mg is below the calculated ~337.5 mg limit, but cumulative dosing must still be tracked
300 mg exceeds a calculated 225 mg limit
questions.explanation: 1% = 10 mg/mL × 30 = 300 mg; 4.5 × 75 ≈ 337 mg. It fits only if no other local anesthetic has been given.

questions.stem: A patient receives 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine for an interscalene block, then the surgeon requests another 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine for infiltration. What cumulative dose must be evaluated against the patient's safe limit?
questions.explanation: 0.5% = 5 mg/mL; 40 mL × 5 = 200 mg total, which must be checked against the weight-based max.

questions.stem: A protocol uses ketamine 0.2 mg/kg then 0.15 mg/kg/hr and magnesium 50 mg/kg then 8 mg/kg/hr. For a 60 kg patient, which set of calculated doses is correct?
options: Ketamine 12 mg then 9 mg/hr; magnesium 3 g then 480 mg/hr
Ketamine 6 mg then 4.5 mg/hr; magnesium 1.5 g then 240 mg/hr
Ketamine 24 mg then 18 mg/hr; magnesium 6 g then 960 mg/hr
Ketamine 12 mg then 90 mg/hr; magnesium 300 mg then 48 mg/hr
questions.explanation: Using the stated protocol: ketamine 0.2 × 60 = 12 mg and 0.15 × 60 = 9 mg/hr; magnesium 50 × 60 = 3,000 mg and 8 × 60 = 480 mg/hr. These are calculations, not universal dosing recommendations.

questions.stem: A PACU patient becomes somnolent with RR 6/min after hydromorphone and midazolam. Which principle best guides immediate management?
options: Support airway and ventilation first, then selectively titrate drug-specific reversal according to the suspected residual effects and patient-specific risks
Flumazenil must always be given before naloxone
Give a large naloxone dose before supporting ventilation
questions.explanation: Airway and ventilation are the immediate priorities. Naloxone and flumazenil can be used selectively when indicated, but there is no universal requirement to reverse the benzodiazepine first; flumazenil itself has important contraindications and seizure risk.

questions.stem: During emergence after laparotomy, an intubated patient is coughing, hypertensive, has dilated pupils, and breathes 26/min with adequate neuromuscular recovery. Which response BEST balances analgesia with extubation safety?
options: Carefully titrate opioid while reassessing ventilation and extubation readiness rather than treating blood pressure alone
Give a large opioid bolus solely to normalize blood pressure
Deepen volatile anesthesia and extubate regardless of readiness
questions.explanation: Coughing, tachypnea, hypertension, and mydriasis may accompany inadequate analgesia but are nonspecific. Titrate analgesia cautiously while reassessing ventilation, anesthetic depth, neuromuscular recovery, and extubation readiness rather than targeting a fixed respiratory rate or pupil size.

questions.stem: A femoral nerve catheter provides excellent resting analgesia, but knee pain prevents participation in physical therapy. Which conclusion BEST guides adjustment of the plan?
options: Analgesic success should include functional pain with movement, not resting pain alone
The block is adequate because resting pain is controlled
Movement-related pain should not influence postoperative analgesia
The catheter should be removed because any movement pain proves block toxicity
questions.explanation: Consider pain with movement and breathing.

questions.stem: A patient reports pain 9/10 while HR is 72/min and BP is 118/70 mm Hg. Which principle should govern the assessment?
options: Normal vital signs do not exclude severe pain; the patient's report remains central
Normal vital signs prove the pain is exaggerated
Analgesia should wait until sympathetic signs develop
Blood pressure is more reliable than self-report
questions.explanation: The best measure is the patient's perception.

questions.stem: Which patient combines both a procedure strongly associated with chronic postsurgical pain and a modifiable perioperative risk factor?
options: A thoracotomy patient with severe poorly controlled acute postoperative pain
A laparoscopic appendectomy patient with effective analgesia
A cataract patient with minimal discomfort
A carpal-tunnel patient with well-controlled pain
questions.explanation: Thoracotomy and poorly controlled acute pain are both strong risk factors for chronic postsurgical pain.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on buprenorphine has severe postoperative pain despite nonopioid adjuncts. Which strategy BEST avoids precipitating withdrawal while treating the new pain burden?
options: Continue buprenorphine and add appropriate full-mu agonist and multimodal therapy as needed
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine may continue with full agonist supplementation.

questions.stem: A physically opioid-dependent patient with only mild sedation receives a large naloxone dose and becomes acutely agitated, hypertensive, and tachycardic. Which error MOST directly caused the deterioration?
options: Excessive antagonist dosing precipitated withdrawal; naloxone should be titrated to the minimum effect needed
questions.explanation: Naloxone can precipitate withdrawal in dependent patients.

questions.stem: A short procedure is induced with a large fentanyl bolus, and the patient remains slow to emerge after the surgery ends quickly. Which planning principle was missed?
options: Match opioid onset, peak, and duration to the intensity and length of surgical stimulation
Use additional opioid at emergence to accelerate redistribution
Prefer long-acting opioids for all short procedures
questions.explanation: Timing and duration must match the procedure.

questions.stem: Ketorolac is given early during a vascular procedure before bleeding risk and surgical hemostasis are clarified. Which planning principle was missed?
options: Coordinate NSAID timing with the surgeon and bleeding context, often near the end of the case
NSAIDs should always be given at induction
NSAID timing is unrelated to surgical bleeding considerations
NSAIDs should replace all opioid therapy
questions.explanation: NSAID use should reflect procedure-specific bleeding risk, renal risk, surgical hemostasis, and team planning. There is no universal rule that NSAIDs can only be given at the end of every operation.

questions.stem: As closure begins after laparoscopic hernia repair, the planned local infiltration has not yet been performed and the cumulative local-anesthetic dose remains acceptable. Which action best preserves the multimodal plan?
options: Prompt the surgeon to perform the planned infiltration before emergence
Replace the infiltration automatically with extra IV opioid
Wait until severe PACU pain develops
Omit local anesthetic because closure has started
questions.explanation: Local infiltration before emergence provides early analgesia and spares opioids.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving dexmedetomidine and hydromorphone and becomes excessively sedated. Which reversal is possible?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine cannot be reversed; opioids can be reversed with naloxone.

questions.stem: Which drug class is recommended for neuropathic components after amputation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain benefits from α2–δ ligands, NMDA antagonists, and α2 agonists.

questions.stem: A PCA patient has reached the programmed 1-hour hydromorphone limit yet continues to report severe pain. Which action BEST distinguishes undertreatment from unsafe escalation?
options: Reassess pain mechanism, sedation, ventilation, PCA use, and the broader analgesic plan before changing settings
Add a large basal infusion without reassessment
Stop the PCA and administer naloxone
questions.explanation: The PCA should be adjusted based on assessment and safety.

questions.stem: After opioid and sedative administration, a patient becomes hypotensive with HR 50/min. Before reflexively giving another analgesic or reversal drug, which immediate assessment best characterizes the hemodynamic problem?
options: Confirm rhythm, blood pressure, perfusion, and medication context
questions.explanation: Assess rhythm and BP before treating bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient with significant renal impairment requires postoperative analgesia. Which strategy BEST minimizes avoidable renal and metabolite-related risk?
options: Acetaminophen plus appropriate regional/nonopioid techniques, with individualized opioid selection if needed
Morphine PCA with a routine basal infusion
questions.explanation: Renal impairment changes the risk-benefit profile of NSAIDs and opioids with renally cleared active metabolites. Acetaminophen, regional techniques, and carefully selected/titrated opioids can reduce avoidable risk; treatment should be individualized rather than assuming all NSAIDs or all renally cleared opioids are absolutely prohibited.

questions.stem: During an IV lidocaine infusion, a patient develops tinnitus and circumoral paresthesia. Which action has priority?
options: Stop lidocaine and evaluate immediately for local-anesthetic systemic toxicity
Increase the infusion because symptoms indicate inadequate effect
Continue unchanged because these are desired analgesic effects
questions.explanation: Tinnitus is an early LAST sign; stop the infusion.

questions.stem: Dexamethasone is planned for both PONV prophylaxis and a modest analgesic benefit during a several-hour case. Which timing principle best supports its use?
options: Administer with enough lead time for its delayed onset to contribute to the intended effects
Wait until PACU because onset is immediate
Avoid it in every patient with diabetes
questions.explanation: The lecture asks when to dose dexamethasone.

questions.stem: A patient with a dense peripheral nerve block is being discharged and fears severe pain when sensation returns overnight. Which instruction BEST prevents a gap in analgesia?
options: Begin the planned oral multimodal regimen before the block fully resolves
Wait until severe pain returns before taking medication
Assume the block will last at least 72 hours
Delay all medication until normal sensation is completely restored
questions.explanation: Educate patients to start analgesics before block resolution.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient takes gabapentin daily and has a neuropathic component to the expected postoperative pain. Which perioperative approach best avoids an unnecessary gap in multimodal therapy?
options: Consider continuing/resuming gabapentin as part of the individualized plan
Stop it routinely one week before surgery
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes continuing vs holding routine meds and multimodal use.

questions.stem: A highly opioid-tolerant patient is rotated to methadone after poor response to escalating doses of another opioid. Which property may make methadone useful beyond simple mu agonism?
options: NMDA-receptor antagonism may help address tolerance/hyperalgesic mechanisms
It is a mixed mu antagonist-kappa agonist
It depends primarily on renal activation
questions.explanation: Methadone is a common rotation choice and also antagonizes NMDA receptors.

questions.stem: A thoracic epidural provides excellent analgesia but the patient becomes hypotensive. Which mechanism should be assessed along with intravascular volume?
questions.explanation: Epidural local anesthetics can cause hypotension via sympathectomy.

questions.stem: A chronic-opioid patient is scheduled for major surgery. Which preoperative step is MOST important before designing supplemental intraoperative and postoperative opioid doses?
options: Determine the baseline daily opioid requirement/equivalent and build a multimodal plan around it
Stop opioids for 48 hours to reduce tolerance
Assume regional anesthesia eliminates the baseline requirement
Give naltrexone to rapidly reverse tolerance
questions.explanation: Tolerant patients need baseline calculation and multimodal plans.

questions.stem: A continuous peripheral nerve catheter becomes disconnected, and a previously comfortable patient develops abrupt severe pain. Which interpretation BEST guides treatment?
options: Loss of continuous regional analgesia caused return or rebound of pain; restore/troubleshoot the block while providing bridge analgesia
The abrupt pain is the expected course and needs no intervention
Stopping local anesthetic caused opioid toxicity
The event indicates local-anesthetic systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Interrupting CPNB causes pain return.

questions.stem: A young woman with high PONV risk undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Which analgesic strategy BEST addresses both pain and a major modifiable PONV contributor?
options: Use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia with appropriate antiemetic prophylaxis
Use high-dose systemic opioid with a basal PCA
Use morphine PCA as the primary strategy
questions.explanation: Multimodal regimens reduce opioid-related PONV.

questions.stem: After bowel surgery, a patient describes diffuse cramping abdominal pain that is difficult to localize and occasionally referred away from the operative site. Which pain type best fits?
questions.explanation: Visceral pain from organs is often poorly localized or referred.

questions.stem: A patient has shooting pain along the leg after spine surgery. What type is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Shooting pain along a nerve distribution suggests peripheral neuropathic pain.

questions.stem: A long-term opioid user reports progressively worse diffuse pain as opioid doses are repeatedly increased. Which possibility should prompt a change in strategy rather than automatic dose escalation?
options: Expected improvement from higher opioid exposure
A need for mixed agonist-antagonists in every patient
questions.explanation: Increasing doses with worsening pain suggest tolerance or hyperalgesia.

questions.stem: A PACU patient has severe acute postoperative pain but will also need sustained analgesia after initial titration. Which prescribing principle is most appropriate?
options: Use a titratable rescue strategy for immediate pain and establish longer-lasting multimodal analgesia appropriate to the procedure and patient
Every PACU patient requires both a short- and long-acting opioid
Use only long-acting opioid so reassessment is unnecessary
Avoid nonopioid analgesia when opioids are prescribed
questions.explanation: Immediate PACU pain often requires carefully titratable rescue therapy, while sustained control should come from an individualized multimodal plan. A long-acting opioid is not mandatory for every PACU patient.

questions.stem: An epidural infusion contains both local anesthetic and opioid. Compared with a local-anesthetic-only technique, which postoperative safety issue requires particular attention?
options: Respiratory depression from neuraxial opioid exposure
No additional monitoring issue once PACU discharge criteria are met
Loss of all motor function regardless of concentration
questions.explanation: Neuraxial opioids change postoperative monitoring requirements.

questions.stem: A family asks why aggressive but safe postoperative pain control matters beyond comfort. Which answer BEST connects analgesia to recovery?
options: Uncontrolled pain can impair pulmonary, cardiovascular, functional, and overall recovery
Pain control changes comfort but not physiologic outcomes
Analgesia primarily shortens the operation itself
Treating pain generally delays mobilization and recovery
questions.explanation: Poorly managed acute pain has multiple adverse physiologic consequences.
